What Is in a 3000 × 3000 Covariance Matrix?

Each face in the notebook is a vector of 3,000 pixels, so its covariance matrix has one row and one column per pixel. Entry (i, j) says how pixels i and j vary together across the 337 faces. Pick a pixel on the average face and see its whole row of the matrix, laid back out as a 60 × 50 picture.

Pixel i

Of all 3,000 pixels, the mouth pixel (52, 27) has the largest variance, 2.381, and the forehead pixel (7, 23) the smallest, 0.210.

Or click, or drag, on the average face. Hover over the map on the right to read single entries; click it to keep pixel j.

What it shows
Row i of the covariance matrix holds the covariance of pixel i with each of the 3,000 pixels. Shown as a picture, it tells you which parts of the face get brighter (red) or darker (blue) when pixel i is brighter than usual. Correlation divides each entry by the two standard deviations, so every value lies between -1 and 1 and pixel i itself scores exactly 1.

    
Back to two dimensions
Any two pixels make a 2D cloud like the one in the deck's first example, with a 2 × 2 covariance matrix: the two variances on the diagonal and Cij off it. The big matrix is all of those 2 × 2 matrices at once. Its eigenvectors, the eigenfaces, are the directions in which the 3,000-dimensional cloud of faces is most stretched.

    
Where the data come from
The notebook's 337 faces, cropped to 60 × 50 ([25:85, 25:75], in sorted file order), each normalized to mean 0 and standard deviation 1. The page recomputes the average face, the centered faces and every entry it shows in the browser, dividing by n - 1 = 336 like the notebook.
